summary.text: Write \(m=2n+1=pd\) for a prime divisor \(p\). If \(p^2\mid m\), then \(1+d\) is coprime to \(m\), has both its \(p\)-th and \(2n\)-th powers equal to \(1\), and hence equals \(1\) modulo \(m\) since \(\gcd(p,2n)=1\), contradicting \(0<d<m\); otherwise \(p\) and \(d\) are coprime, and a hypothetical \(b^n=-1\) yields by CRT a unit \(c\equiv b\pmod p\), \(c\equiv1\pmod d\), whose \(n\)-th power can be neither \(+1\) modulo \(p\) nor \(-1\) modulo \(d\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
m=2n+1.
\]
By hypothesis, \(m\) is an absolute Euler pseudoprime. Thus \(m>1\), \(m\) is not prime, and for every integer \(u\) coprime to \(m\),
\[
u^{(m-1)/2}\equiv 1\pmod m
\quad\text{or}\quad
u^{(m-1)/2}\equiv -1\pmod m.
\]
Since \(m=2n+1\), we have \((m-1)/2=n\). Consequently,
\[
\gcd(u,m)=1\implies u^n\equiv \pm1\pmod m. \tag{1}
\]
Also, \(m>1\) implies \(n\geq 1\), and \(m\) is odd.

We will prove that there is no integer \(b\) satisfying
\[
b^n\equiv -1\pmod m. \tag{2}
\]
This is stronger than necessary, since the sequence only counts such \(b\) in the range \(1\leq b<m\).

We use twice the elementary fact that, for a positive modulus \(q\),
\[
-1\equiv 1\pmod q\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q\mid 2. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, subtracting the two sides says that \(2\equiv0\pmod q\).

Choose a prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\), which exists because \(m>1\), and put
\[
d=\frac mp.
\]
Then
\[
m=pd. \tag{4}
\]
Because \(m\) is odd, \(p\neq2\), so in particular \(p\geq3\). We divide the argument into two cases according as \(p^2\) does or does not divide \(m\).

### Case 1: \(p^2\mid m\)

In this case \(p\mid d\), because \(m=pd\). Consider the residue
\[
x=1+d\pmod m.
\]
First, \(x\) is a unit modulo \(m\), or equivalently \(\gcd(1+d,m)=1\). To see this, suppose that a prime \(q\) divided both \(1+d\) and \(m=pd\). Since \(q\) is prime and divides \(pd\), either \(q\mid p\) or \(q\mid d\). In the first alternative, since both \(q\) and \(p\) are prime, \(q=p\); but \(p\mid d\), so this again gives \(q\mid d\). Thus in every case \(q\mid d\). Since also \(q\mid1+d\), it follows that \(q\mid(1+d)-d=1\), which is impossible. Hence no prime divides both \(1+d\) and \(m\), proving the claim.

Next observe that
\[
d^2\equiv0\pmod m. \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, \(p\mid d\), so \(pd=m\) divides \(d^2\).

Whenever an element \(t\) of a commutative ring satisfies \(t^2=0\), one has
\[
(1+t)^k=1+kt \tag{6}
\]
for every nonnegative integer \(k\). This follows directly by induction: the assertion is clear for \(k=0\), and if it holds for \(k\), then
\[
(1+t)^{k+1}=(1+kt)(1+t)=1+(k+1)t+kt^2=1+(k+1)t.
\]
Apply this in \(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\) with \(t=d\) and \(k=p\). By (5) and \(pd=m\),
\[
x^p=(1+d)^p\equiv1+pd\equiv1\pmod m. \tag{7}
\]
On the other hand, since \(x\) is coprime to \(m\), property (1) gives \(x^n\equiv1\) or \(x^n\equiv-1\pmod m\). Squaring either possibility yields
\[
x^{2n}\equiv1\pmod m. \tag{8}
\]

Let \(r\) be the multiplicative order of the unit \(x\) modulo \(m\). From (7), \(r\mid p\), and from (8), \(r\mid2n\). But
\[
\gcd(p,2n)=1. \tag{9}
\]
Indeed, \(p\mid m=2n+1\); if \(p\) also divided \(2n\), it would divide their difference \(1\), which is impossible. Since \(r\) divides both relatively prime integers \(p\) and \(2n\), we get \(r=1\). Therefore \(x\equiv1\pmod m\). As \(x=1+d\), this implies
\[
d\equiv0\pmod m,
\]
so \(m\mid d\).

This is impossible. In fact, from \(m=pd\), with \(m>0\) and \(p\geq3\), we have \(d>0\) and \(d<m\). No positive integer strictly smaller than \(m\) can be divisible by \(m\). Thus the case \(p^2\mid m\) is incompatible with the absolute Euler property.

### Case 2: \(p^2\nmid m\)

Now \(p\) and \(d\) are coprime. Indeed, because \(p\) is prime, failure of coprimality would imply \(p\mid d\), and then \(p^2\mid pd=m\), contrary to the present assumption.

We also have
\[
d>1. \tag{10}
\]
Certainly \(d>0\), since \(m=pd>0\). If \(d=1\), then (4) would give \(m=p\), making \(m\) prime, contrary to the definition of an absolute Euler pseudoprime.

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that an integer \(b\) satisfies (2). Because \(n\geq1\), in the ring \(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\) we may write
\[
b\bigl(-b^{n-1}\bigr)=-b^n\equiv1\pmod m.
\]
Thus \(b\) is a unit modulo \(m\), and hence
\[
\gcd(b,m)=1. \tag{11}
\]
Since \(p\mid m\), it follows in particular that \(\gcd(b,p)=1\). Reducing (2) modulo \(p\) gives
\[
b^n\equiv-1\pmod p. \tag{12}
\]

Because \(p\) and \(d\) are coprime, the Chinese remainder theorem supplies an integer \(c\) such that
\[
c\equiv b\pmod p,
\qquad
c\equiv1\pmod d. \tag{13}
\]
This \(c\) is coprime to \(m=pd\). Indeed, the first congruence and \(\gcd(b,p)=1\) show that \(\gcd(c,p)=1\), while the second congruence shows that \(\gcd(c,d)=1\). Therefore no prime factor of \(pd\) divides \(c\), so
\[
\gcd(c,m)=1. \tag{14}
\]
Applying the absolute Euler property (1) to \(c\), there are two possibilities:
\[
c^n\equiv1\pmod m
\quad\text{or}\quad
c^n\equiv-1\pmod m. \tag{15}
\]
We show that both are impossible.

If \(c^n\equiv1\pmod m\), reduce this congruence modulo \(p\). Since \(c\equiv b\pmod p\), it gives
\[
b^n\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Together with (12), this yields \(-1\equiv1\pmod p\). By (3), \(p\mid2\), impossible because \(p\geq3\).

If instead \(c^n\equiv-1\pmod m\), reduce modulo \(d\). Since \(c\equiv1\pmod d\), we obtain
\[
1=c^n\equiv-1\pmod d.
\]
By (3), this forces \(d\mid2\). But \(d>1\), so this would imply \(d=2\). That is impossible because \(d\mid m\) by (4), whereas \(m=2n+1\) is odd. Thus the second possibility is impossible as well.

Both alternatives in (15) lead to contradictions. Hence no \(b\) can satisfy (2).

It follows that the set
\[
\{b\in\{1,2,\ldots,2n\}: b^n\equiv-1\pmod{2n+1}\}
\]
is empty. Its cardinality is therefore zero, which is exactly
\[
a(n)=0.
\]
